title: Lachman Test for ACL Tears
purpose: Detect anterior cruciate ligament (ACL) tears; described as the most valid ACL test (also called Ritchie, Trillat or Lachman-Trillat test).
structure: Anterior cruciate ligament; anterior tibial translation at 30° flexion. Exclude a PCL injury first, since a posteriorly sagging tibia can create a false-positive impression of excess anterior translation.
procedure: Patient supine, knee at 30° flexion. Fixate the femur with one hand, bring the tibia into slight external rotation and translate the tibia anteriorly with the other hand.
positive: Soft or mushy end-feel, or anterior tibial translation at least 3 mm greater than the uninjured side.

accuracy.source: Benjaminse et al. 2006 meta-analysis (also cited: van Eck 2013, Huang 2016, Lange 2015)

notes: Results are more valid in chronic than acute situations because swelling and muscle spasm degrade testing. Other ACL tests: anterior drawer, Lelli/lever sign, lateral pivot shift.

title: Anterior Drawer Test to Assess ACL Injuries
structure: Anterior cruciate ligament; anterior tibial translation at 90° flexion. Exclude a PCL injury first to avoid false positives.
procedure: Hip 45°, knee 90° flexion; fixate by gently sitting on the patient's foot. Palpate the joint line with the thumbs and pull the tibia anteriorly in an explosive movement.
positive: Anterior tibial translation greater than 6 mm, or a soft, mushy end-feel.

accuracy.source: Benjaminse et al. 2006 meta-analysis; performs far worse in acute injuries

notes: Other ACL tests: Lachman, lateral pivot shift, Lelli/lever sign. Also cited: van Eck 2013, Huang 2016, Peeler 2010.

title: Lateral Pivot-Shift Test for ACL Ruptures
purpose: Detect ACL rupture by reproducing the dynamic anterior subluxation of the lateral tibial plateau that occurs at 20-40° knee flexion during gait in an ACL-deficient knee.
structure: Anterior cruciate ligament and anterolateral compartment; iliotibial band reduces the subluxed tibia at 30-40° flexion.
procedure: Patient supine, hip flexed and abducted 30° in slight medial rotation. Hold the leg at the calcaneus and internally rotate the tibia (some authors add axial compression); apply a valgus force from behind the fibula with the other hand, which subluxates the tibia anteriorly in extension. Slowly flex the knee.
positive: The tibia reduces or jogs backward at about 30-40° flexion as the iliotibial band tightens, often with a clunk; the patient recognizes the 'giving way' feeling.
notes: Protective muscle contraction in acute injuries can cause false negatives: have the patient relax and repeat a few times. Other ACL tests: Lachman, Lelli/lever sign, anterior drawer.

title: Lever Sign or Lelli's Test | ACL Rupture Assessment
purpose: Newer test of ACL integrity using the leg as a lever over a fist placed under the calf.
structure: Anterior cruciate ligament; with a torn ACL the lever that offsets gravity is impaired and the tibial plateau translates anteriorly on the femoral condyles.
procedure: Patient supine with the leg fully extended. Place a fist under the proximal third of the calf and apply moderate downward force to the distal third of the quadriceps.
positive: Intact ACL: the knee extends and the heel rises off the table (negative). Partial or complete rupture: the heel stays on the table (positive).

accuracy.source: Lelli et al. 2016 (high risk of bias, author is the test's founder); Jarbo et al. 2017; also cited Mulligan 2017, Gürpınar 2019, Massey 2017

notes: Page rates moderate clinical value for confirming ACL tears. Other ACL tests: anterior drawer, Lachman, lateral pivot shift.

title: Jerk Test Knee | Anterior Cruciate Ligament Tear
purpose: Test ACL integrity together with the anterolateral compartment (Hughston et al. 1976); essentially a pivot shift performed in the reverse order of movements.
structure: Anterior cruciate ligament and anterolateral compartment; lateral tibial plateau.
procedure: Patient supine, hip 45° and knee 90° flexion. One hand applies internal tibial rotation, the other hand over the proximal tibial plateau and fibula applies a valgus force. Slowly extend the knee.
positive: A sudden acceleration or jerk, usually around 30° flexion, from anterior subluxation of the lateral tibial plateau; the tibia reduces again at full extension.

accuracy.source: n/a: no diagnostic accuracy assessment (Hughston 1976; Jensen 1990)

notes: Clinical value questionable. Other ACL tests: anterior drawer, Lachman, lateral pivot shift.

title: Losee Test | Anterior Cruciate Ligament Tear
purpose: Pivot-shift variant (Losee et al. 1978) for the anterior subluxation of the lateral tibial plateau typical of ACL-deficient knees.
structure: Anterior cruciate ligament; lateral tibial plateau; fibular head.
procedure: Patient supine, examiner on the side examined (described for the left knee). Hold the foot and ankle with the left hand in external rotation, brace the leg against the abdomen, and flex the knee to 30° so the hamstrings relax (external rotation reduces the subluxation at the start). Place the right hand on the knee with the thumb hooked behind the fibular head; apply valgus by pulling the foot laterally and pushing medially with the right hand. Maintaining valgus, slowly extend the leg letting it internally rotate while pushing the fibular head forward with the thumb.
positive: Anterior subluxation of the knee, which the patient recognizes as their feeling of instability.

accuracy.source: n/a: no formal diagnostic accuracy assessment (Losee 1978; Anderson 2000)

notes: Clinical value questionable. Other ACL tests: anterior drawer, Lachman, lateral pivot shift.

title: Martens' Test | Anterior Cruciate Ligament Tear
purpose: Test for anterior subluxation of the tibia (Martens et al. 1981), claimed to avoid apprehension and muscle spasm and thus false negatives.
structure: Anterior cruciate ligament; lateral tibial plateau.
procedure: Patient supine, lower leg braced between the examiner's arm and body, one hand behind the proximal tibia and the other on the distal femur. Step 1: Lachman manoeuvre, pulling the tibia anteriorly and the femur posteriorly (straight anterior subluxation appears in an ACL-deficient knee). Step 2: add valgus torque through the elbow at the ankle plus internal tibial rotation.
positive: A sudden snap of varying degree felt or seen as the tibia subluxes anteriorly.

accuracy.source: n/a: not formally assessed against a reference standard (Martens & Mulier 1981)

notes: Clinical value questionable. Other ACL tests: anterior drawer, Lachman, lateral pivot shift.

title: Dejour Test | Anterior Cruciate Ligament (ACL) Tear Assessment
purpose: ACL test combining features of the Lachman test and the pivot shift.
structure: Anterior cruciate ligament; tibial plateau; posteromedial corner (PMC) judged by the quality of the pivot shift.
procedure: Patient supine, examiner on the examined side holding the leg loosely between arm and abdomen to allow tibial rotation. Apply valgus with the forearm and push the femur posteriorly with the other hand to accentuate the anterior drawer, which appears at 20-30° flexion; flex further.
positive: A pivot shift occurs with further flexion: sudden reduction of the anterior tibial subluxation. Per Dejour, a violent painful pivot shift means the PMC is intact; a sluggish one suggests PMC insufficiency.
notes: Clinical value questionable. Other ACL tests: anterior drawer, Lachman, lateral pivot shift.

title: Jolt Test / Nakajima N-Test | Anterior Cruciate Ligament Tear
purpose: Pivot-shift-like test (Nakajima's n-test) reproducing the jolt of an ACL-deficient knee.
structure: Anterior cruciate ligament; tibial plateau; fibular head.
procedure: Patient supine, knee 90° flexion (described for the right knee). Right hand grasps the lateral ankle and applies internal rotation; left hand on the lateral knee applies valgus with the thumb on the posterior fibular head. Gradually extend the knee.
positive: Sudden anterior-medial subluxation of the tibial plateau with a palpable jolt, usually around 40-20° from extension; the patient may recognize the 'giving way' sensation.

accuracy.source: n/a: no diagnostic accuracy assessment (Nakajima; page text says 1972, reference list says 1979)

notes: Clinical value questionable. Other ACL tests: anterior drawer, Lachman, lateral pivot shift.

title: Slocum Test | Anterolateral Rotatory Instability
purpose: Side-lying modification of the lateral pivot shift (Slocum 1976) to test ACL integrity / anterolateral rotatory instability, designed for heavier patients.
structure: Anterior cruciate ligament; anterolateral compartment; gravity produces internal rotation and anterior subluxation of the tibia.
procedure: Patient side-lying on the unaffected side, lower hip and knee slightly flexed, pelvis rotated about 30° posteriorly, ankle of the affected leg resting on the table, knee flexed 10°. Place one hand above and one below the knee, apply valgus and bring the knee into flexion.
positive: Sudden reduction of the tibia at around 40° knee flexion.

accuracy.source: n/a: not included in diagnostic accuracy studies (Slocum et al. 1976)

notes: Clinical value questionable. Other rotatory instability tests: giving way, crossover, Lemaire jolt, reverse pivot shift, dial, frog leg.

title: Cross Over Test | Anterolateral Rotatory Instability
purpose: Weight-bearing test for anterolateral rotatory instability proposed by Arnold (1979) for athletic patients in whom muscular guarding makes the pivot shift or jerk test difficult.
structure: Anterior cruciate ligament / anterolateral compartment under weight bearing and torso rotation.
procedure: Patient standing, crosses the unaffected leg over the affected leg keeping the affected foot flat on the floor. The examiner gently steps on the affected foot to fixate it and asks the patient to rotate the torso as far as possible with the quadriceps contracted.
positive: Reproduction of a lateral pivot shift and the symptom of 'the knee wanting to go out'.

accuracy.source: n/a: no diagnostic accuracy studies (Arnold et al. 1979)

notes: Clinical value questionable. Other rotatory instability tests: Slocum, giving way (Jakob), Lemaire jolt (anteromedial), reverse pivot shift, dial, frog leg (posterolateral).

title: Giving Way Test | Anterolateral Rotatory Instability
purpose: Standing test (Jakob et al. 1981) to reproduce anterior subluxation of the lateral tibial plateau, possibly easier to elicit in muscular or guarding patients than non-weight-bearing tests.
structure: Anterior cruciate ligament / anterolateral compartment under weight bearing.
procedure: Patient standing with the unaffected side leaning against a wall or table but weight distributed equally. The examiner places the hands above and below the knee, applies valgus and moves the knee into flexion.
positive: Valgus plus flexion elicits a jerk and the knee gives way; the patient may recognize the instability feeling.

accuracy.source: n/a: not compared with a reference test (Jakob et al. 1981)

notes: Clinical value questionable. Other rotatory instability tests: Slocum, crossover, Lemaire jolt, reverse pivot shift, dial, frog leg.

title: Lemaire Jolt Test | Anteromedial Rotatory Instability
purpose: Lemaire's (1967) test to confirm ACL rupture, described as excellent in the anaesthetized patient; hard to elicit in awake patients who cannot fully relax.
structure: Anterior cruciate ligament; anteromedial subluxation of the tibia; fibular head and biceps femoris tendon.
procedure: Patient supine, examiner on the examined side. One hand at the ankle holds the extended leg in internal rotation; the dorsum of the other hand is placed behind the fibular head and biceps femoris tendon to apply a ventrally directed force. The patient relaxes completely; the knee is gently flexed and extended repeatedly while observing for anteromedial tibial subluxation. Step 2: increase the flexion angle.
positive: The tibia jolts backward as the flexion angle increases.

accuracy.source: n/a: not assessed for diagnostic ability (Liorzou 2013)

notes: Clinical value questionable. Page heading says anteromedial rotatory instability while the text also mentions anterolateral instability being hard to elicit awake. Other rotatory instability tests: Slocum, giving way, crossover, reverse pivot shift, dial, frog leg.
